rw: A datasheet documents how a data set was collected, what it contains and its limits, which helps users judge whether the data suits their purpose and avoid misuse.

ww.A spreadsheet of results from a data set: A results spreadsheet with column totals reports outputs of analysis, but it does not document how the data was collected, what it contains or its limits.
ww.A sheet that lists prices of the goods t: A price list for goods sold to customers is a commercial catalog, and it says nothing about the origin, contents or limitations of any data set.
ww.A sheet that lists employees and their p: A list of employees and their monthly pay is a payroll record, which has no link to describing the provenance or quality of a data set.

rw: Under GDPR a person may ask a controller to erase their personal data in certain cases, for example when it is no longer needed or consent is withdrawn.

ww.The right to forget passwords, so a user: The right to be forgotten concerns personal data held by organizations, not memory of passwords, so a user still needs credentials or a reset process to log in.
ww.The right to delete other people's data: The right applies only to a person's own personal data and only in certain cases, so it gives no power to delete other people's data whenever it seems wrong.
ww.The right to remove laws that a user doe: GDPR gives individuals rights over their personal data and does not let anyone repeal laws, which only the legislature of the state can do.

rw: Data portability lets people receive their personal data in a structured, usable format and transfer it to another service, which supports user choice and competition between providers.

ww.Carrying a computer from one place to an: Moving a computer in a bag or on a trolley is physical portability of hardware, and it has nothing to do with the rights people hold over their data.
ww.Deleting data from a database by running: Running a command that removes all rows is data deletion, which erases records, while portability is about handing the data to the person to reuse elsewhere.
ww.Selling data to other firms for a fee af: Selling data to other firms is a commercial transfer for a fee, whereas portability is a right of the individual to take their own data to another service.

rw: A DPO is the person responsible for overseeing an organization's data protection compliance, advising on duties, monitoring practices and acting as the contact point for regulators.

ww.A salesperson who sells data products to: A salesperson sells data products and serves customers, which is a commercial role, while a DPO monitors compliance and advises on legal duties about personal data.
ww.A guard for a data center who checks the: A guard who checks visitor badges handles physical security of a building, which differs from the advisory and compliance role that the law gives a DPO.
ww.A programmer who writes the code for the: A programmer writes code for storage systems, but a DPO is not defined by building software and instead oversees whether data handling follows the law.

rw: Pseudonymization swaps identifying fields for artificial identifiers, so data is less directly identifiable, though it can still be linked back to a person using separately kept additional information.

ww.Publishing names and details of the peop: Publishing names and details of people on a public website exposes personal data, which is the opposite of reducing how identifiable the people in the data are.
ww.Deleting all data about a person from ev: Deleting all data about a person from every system and backup is erasure, which removes the data entirely, while pseudonymization keeps the data with its identifiers replaced.
ww.Encrypting a network so that only approv: Encrypting a network limits which devices connect and hides traffic, which is a security measure, but it does not replace identifying fields inside the data itself.

rw: Purpose limitation means personal data is used only for the purposes stated at collection, so people know what to expect and the data is not reused unrelated ways.

ww.Collecting data for any use the firm lik: Collecting data for any use at any time from any source is the opposite of purpose limitation, which restricts use to purposes stated when the data was gathered.
ww.Limiting the number of users who may log: Capping how many users can log in at once concerns system capacity and access control, not the purposes for which personal data may later be used.
ww.Limiting the size of a data set so it us: Keeping a data set small to save disk space is about storage size, whereas purpose limitation concerns why the data is used, not how much space it needs.

rw: A data subject is the identified or identifiable person whom personal data is about, and that person holds rights such as access, correction and erasure.

ww.The topic of a report or a study here: The topic of a report is its subject matter, which is a different idea from the data subject, who is the individual that personal data identifies.
ww.The programmer who wrote the code: The programmer who wrote the code is a developer of the system, and holds no special status simply for building software that processes the data.
ww.The owner of the database and its record: The owner of a database is usually the controller or organization holding the records, which is the party bound by duties toward the data subject, not the subject.

rw: A proxy variable is a feature that stands in for a protected trait, such as a postcode reflecting race, so a model can discriminate even when the trait is removed.

ww.A variable with missing values in many r: A variable with many missing values has a data quality problem that needs imputation, but being incomplete does not mean it stands in for a protected trait.
ww.A variable with the largest value in a d: A variable holding the largest value in a data set is merely an outlier, and its size does not make it a stand-in for a protected trait.
ww.A variable stored on a proxy server so u: A proxy server is a network intermediary for web traffic, which is a different meaning of proxy and has no connection to a feature that correlates with protected traits.

rw: Disparate impact arises when a policy or model seems neutral on its face but disproportionately harms a protected group, even without any intent to discriminate.

ww.A policy with no effect on any group, so: A policy with no effect on any group helps or harms nobody, so it cannot cause the unequal harm that defines disparate impact on a protected group.
ww.A policy that harms everyone equally, so: A policy harming everyone equally affects no group more than another, so it lacks the unequal burden on a protected group that disparate impact describes.
ww.A policy that helps a group of people mo: A policy that helps a group because of a trait they hold describes preferential treatment, not a neutral policy that unintentionally harms a protected group.

rw: In a bias-amplifying feedback loop, a system's output shapes future data, so an existing pattern is reinforced, as when predictive policing sends officers back to the same areas.

ww.A loop in code with no end, so that a pr: An infinite loop in code repeats a step forever, which is a programming bug and has nothing to do with outputs shaping future data and reinforcing bias.
ww.A loop of wires that carries current aro: A loop of wire carrying current around a circuit is an electrical idea, and it does not describe how model outputs feed back into data and amplify bias.
ww.A loop in a chart where a line curves ba: A chart line that curves back and crosses itself is a visual feature of a plot, not a process in which results change later data.

rw: Documenting data and models, testing for bias and keeping humans in the loop give transparency, accountability and oversight, which are the core practices behind trustworthy AI.

ww.Skipping tests to save time and money, s: Skipping tests removes the checks that find bias, errors and safety problems, so it undermines trust in AI instead of building it, despite saving time.
ww.Collecting as much data as possible in c: Gathering as much data as possible just in case breaks data minimization, raises privacy risk and does nothing to make a system more trustworthy or fair.
ww.Hiding how the system works from users,: Hiding how a system works from users, auditors and regulators removes transparency and accountability, which are needed for trust, so this practice erodes trustworthiness.

rw: Generative text can contain errors or invented facts, sometimes called hallucinations, so unchecked use can spread false information, which is the main risk.

ww.It cannot be edited by any human user: AI-generated text can be edited by people like any other text, so being uneditable is not a real risk of using it.
ww.It will always be perfect and never err: AI text is not always perfect, since models make mistakes, and the claim that it never errs is the very assumption that makes unchecked use risky.
ww.It is illegal to read in most countries: Reading AI-generated text is not illegal in most countries, so legality of reading is not the main risk, whereas inaccuracy is.

rw: An AI impact assessment reviews how a system may affect people, rights and safety before and during use, so risks can be found and reduced early.

ww.A test of how fast a model runs on a com: Measuring model speed and memory use is a performance benchmark, which says nothing about how the system might affect people, their rights or their safety.
ww.A cost estimate only, listing what it wi: A cost estimate of hardware and software looks only at money, and an impact assessment instead examines possible harms and benefits to the people the system affects.
ww.A marketing plan for selling the system: A marketing plan with prices and ads is meant to sell the system, whereas an impact assessment looks critically at its effects on people and rights.

rw: A hospital is a facility that provides inpatient and emergency medical care, with beds, doctors, nurses and equipment available around the clock for serious conditions.

ww.A store that sells medicine without a pr: A store selling medicine over the counter is a retail pharmacy, which does not offer the inpatient and emergency care that define a hospital.
ww.A school that trains medical students on: A school that trains students only is an educational institution, and a hospital by definition treats patients, so this description leaves out the central purpose.
ww.An office that only handles insurance fo: An office handling only insurance forms and claims is an administrative or billing function, which supports care but does not deliver inpatient or emergency treatment.

rw: A primary care provider handles routine care and coordinates a patient's other care, acting as the usual first contact and referring to specialists when needed.

ww.A surgeon who performs only emergency op: A surgeon performing only emergency operations in a trauma unit is a specialist, whereas a primary care provider handles routine, ongoing care across many conditions.
ww.A pharmacist who fills prescriptions and: A pharmacist fills prescriptions and advises on medicines, which is an important role but not the patient's first point of contact who coordinates care.
ww.A manager who sets hospital budgets and: A manager setting budgets and signing wage bills does administrative work, which is unrelated to delivering and coordinating a patient's medical care.

rw: A specialist focuses on one area of medicine, such as heart or skin conditions, and has advanced training in that field beyond general care.

ww.Manages the front desk of a clinic and a: Managing a clinic's front desk and answering phones is an administrative job, not a clinical role that diagnoses or treats a particular area of medicine.
ww.Orders supplies for a hospital and check: Ordering hospital supplies and checking storeroom stock is a materials management task, which has nothing to do with focused medical care for patients.
ww.Handles every kind of illness for all pa: Handling every kind of illness from colds to rare diseases describes a generalist, while a specialist narrows to one area to treat complex problems.

rw: An outpatient service gives care that does not require staying overnight in a hospital, so the patient visits for treatment or tests and goes home.

ww.Care provided only in an emergency room: Care given only in an emergency room is emergency care, which is one setting, whereas outpatient service covers many visits that do not need an overnight stay.
ww.Care that requires a stay of several nig: Care requiring several nights in a hospital bed is inpatient care, which is the opposite of an outpatient service that sends the patient home.
ww.Care provided by a patient to themselves: Care a patient provides for themselves at home is self-care without staff, whereas outpatient service is delivered by professionals at a facility.

rw: An inpatient is a patient formally admitted to a hospital, usually staying at least one night, so that doctors and nurses can treat and monitor them.

ww.A patient who visits a clinic for an app: A patient who visits a clinic and goes home that day is an outpatient, so this description reverses the meaning of inpatient.
ww.A patient who calls the office for advic: A patient phoning the office for advice or a booking slot is not admitted and does not stay in the hospital, so is not an inpatient.
ww.A patient who only fills prescriptions a: A patient who only fills prescriptions at a pharmacy counter has no hospital admission, so that person is a pharmacy customer and not an inpatient.

rw: A long-term care facility provides ongoing care for people who cannot live fully independently, such as older adults or people with serious disabilities, often with help for daily tasks.

ww.A lab that tests blood samples and tissu: A lab that tests blood and tissue samples is a diagnostic service, which analyzes specimens but does not give ongoing residential care to people who need help daily.
ww.A clinic that treats minor cuts and spra: A clinic treating minor cuts and sprains for walk-in patients is urgent care, which gives short episodes of treatment, not continuing care over months or years.
ww.An office that prints medical forms and: An office that prints and files medical forms does clerical work, so it provides no nursing, personal care or living support for dependent residents.

rw: Urgent care is walk-in treatment for problems that need prompt attention but are not life threatening, such as sprains, minor cuts or infections, without an appointment.

ww.Care for patients who need major surgery: Care for major surgery with a long intensive care stay is acute hospital care, which differs from urgent care for problems that are not life threatening.
ww.Care that is provided at home for chroni: Home care for chronic illness by visiting nurses is home health care, and urgent care instead is a walk-in service at a facility for sudden problems.
ww.Care only available by appointment weeks: Care available only by appointment weeks ahead is routine scheduled care, whereas urgent care takes walk-ins who need to be seen promptly.

rw: Home health care is medical or nursing services delivered to a patient at home, such as wound care, therapy or monitoring, so people can recover in familiar surroundings.

ww.Care delivered only inside a hospital wa: Care delivered only inside a hospital ward is inpatient care, so it cannot be home health care, which takes place where the patient lives.
ww.Care that requires patients to travel fa: Requiring patients to travel far to a clinic is the reverse of home health care, which brings services to the patient instead of the patient to a facility.
ww.Care that patients give to their pets at: Pets receiving care at home from their owners is not health care for patients, since home health care means clinical services given to people.

rw: Hospice care is comfort-focused care for people near the end of life, easing pain and symptoms and supporting the patient and family rather than seeking a cure.

ww.Care for newborn babies only, in a unit: Care only for newborn babies in a unit for the very young is neonatal care, which is a different service from end-of-life comfort care.
ww.Care that replaces all insurance for tho: Hospice is a type of care, not an insurance substitute, and it does not replace all coverage for those who cannot pay for services.
ww.Care aimed at curing every illness until: Care aimed at curing every illness until recovery describes curative treatment, whereas hospice accepts that cure is no longer the goal and focuses on comfort.

rw: A for-profit hospital is owned by investors and aims to earn a profit, which may be paid to owners or shareholders as returns.

ww.A hospital owned by the government and r: A hospital owned by the government and run with public money is a public hospital, which differs from one owned by private investors seeking profit.
ww.A hospital run by a religious order, wit: A hospital run by a religious order with no aim of profit is a nonprofit hospital, not a for-profit one owned by investors.
ww.A hospital that charges nothing to any p: A hospital that charges nothing to any patient is a charity model, which cannot earn profit, so it contradicts the for-profit definition.

rw: A nonprofit hospital reinvests surplus revenue into its mission, such as care, equipment and community programs, rather than paying out profits to owners.

ww.A hospital owned by investors who take p: A hospital owned by investors who take profits and pay dividends is for-profit, whereas a nonprofit hospital does not distribute earnings to owners or shareholders.
ww.A hospital that never earns revenue and: Nonprofit hospitals do earn revenue from patient care and insurers, and a surplus is allowed, so saying they never earn revenue and live on gifts is false.
ww.A hospital closed to the public and open: A hospital closed to the public and open only to staff and relatives is a private facility by access, which says nothing about how profits are used.

rw: The CEO is responsible for overall operations and strategy, guiding leaders, finances and quality so the hospital meets its mission and serves its community.

ww.Only filling the prescriptions: Filling prescriptions is the work of pharmacists, and the CEO has a much wider remit than one task like dispensing medicines.
ww.Only cleaning patient rooms: Cleaning patient rooms is the task of housekeeping staff, while the CEO is responsible for running the entire organization, so this is far too narrow.
ww.Only sending bills to patients: Sending bills to patients is a billing office function, and the CEO oversees the whole hospital, not only the single task of invoicing.

rw: The governing board oversees the hospital's mission, policies and top leadership, including hiring the CEO, and holds the organization accountable to the community it serves.

ww.Prepares meals for patients in the kitch: Preparing patient meals is done by the dietary or kitchen staff, which is an operational task, not the governance role of a board.
ww.Schedules appointments at the front desk: Scheduling appointments and answering phones is front desk work, which a governing board does not do because it sets direction, not daily office tasks.
ww.Provides daily nursing care at the bedsi: Bedside nursing care is given by nurses on the wards, whereas the governing board has no role in the hands-on care of individual patients.

rw: A department is a unit focused on a particular service, such as radiology or pharmacy, with its own staff, equipment and manager within the hospital.

ww.A building that is separate from the hos: A separate building with its own address is a different facility or campus, whereas a department is a unit inside the hospital that serves one function.
ww.A form patients sign on arrival to give: A consent form signed on arrival is a document, not an organizational unit, so it cannot be a department of the hospital.
ww.A type of medical insurance that pays pa: Insurance that pays part of a patient's bill is a financing arrangement, which has nothing to do with the hospital's internal organization into units.

rw: Radiology takes and reads medical images such as X-rays, CT scans and MRI, helping doctors diagnose injuries and disease inside the body.

ww.Provides physical rehabilitation and the: Providing physical rehabilitation and therapy is the work of the physical therapy department, which helps patients regain movement, not make or read medical images.
ww.Tests blood and tissue samples for disea: Testing blood and tissue samples for disease is done by the clinical laboratory, not radiology, which relies on imaging equipment instead of specimens.
ww.Prepares and dispenses medicines on the: Preparing and dispensing medicines on the wards is the job of the pharmacy department, which works with drugs, not images.

rw: A clinical laboratory tests samples such as blood and urine to help diagnose illness, giving doctors results that guide treatment decisions.

ww.Prepares meals for patients in the kitch: Preparing and delivering patient meals is food service work, which has no connection with analyzing body samples in a laboratory.
ww.Handles billing questions from patients: Handling billing questions from patients and insurers is done by the billing or finance office, not by a laboratory that analyzes specimens.
ww.Takes X-ray pictures of the bones and ch: Taking X-ray pictures of bones and the chest is the work of radiology, which uses imaging machines, whereas the laboratory tests samples.

rw: The pharmacy department prepares and dispenses medications and advises on their use, helping make sure patients get the right drug, dose and instructions safely.

ww.Performs surgery on patients in the oper: Performing surgery in operating rooms is done by surgeons and surgical teams, while the pharmacy department deals with medications and not with operations.
ww.Processes insurance claims for payment f: Processing insurance claims for payment is done by billing and finance staff, a business function that has no part in preparing medicines.
ww.Cleans operating rooms after surgery and: Cleaning operating rooms and sterilizing tools is done by environmental services and sterile processing, which is a different department from the pharmacy.

rw: A registered nurse provides patient care, administers medications and educates patients, while monitoring their condition and working with doctors in the care team.

ww.Repairs medical equipment such as beds,: Repairing beds, monitors and scanners is the work of biomedical or maintenance technicians, not a registered nurse, whose duties center on patient care.
ww.Sets the hospital's annual budget and ap: Setting the annual budget and approving departmental spending is a task for executives and finance leaders, not for nurses providing bedside care.
ww.Handles insurance contracts for the hosp: Handling insurance contracts and setting doctors' pay is administrative and financial work done by management, which sits outside a registered nurse's clinical role.

rw: A physician assistant is a licensed clinician who diagnoses and treats patients under a collaborative arrangement with physicians, performing exams, ordering tests and prescribing medicine.

ww.A hospital volunteer who delivers flower: A volunteer who delivers flowers, mail and magazines gives comfort to patients but holds no clinical license and does not diagnose or treat illness.
ww.A billing clerk who files claims with in: A billing clerk files claims with insurers and follows up on unpaid ones, which is a financial task unrelated to diagnosing and treating patients.
ww.A receptionist who schedules visits and: A receptionist schedules visits and greets patients at the desk, an administrative role that lacks the clinical training and license of a physician assistant.

rw: A medical assistant supports clinicians with tasks such as taking vital signs and scheduling, helping clinics run smoothly under supervision of providers.

ww.Setting national health policy for the g: Setting national health policy belongs to governments and ministries, which is far beyond the practical clinic tasks that a medical assistant carries out.
ww.Running the hospital board and chairing: Running the hospital board and chairing its meetings is a governance function for trustees and officers, not the role of a medical assistant.
ww.Performing major surgeries alone in the: Performing major surgeries alone is beyond a medical assistant's training and license, since surgery is done by surgeons with advanced education and credentials.

rw: A health unit coordinator manages communication and paperwork on a hospital unit, such as handling orders, charts, phone calls and messages between staff.

ww.Taking X-rays of the chest and bones of: Taking X-rays of the chest and bones is done by radiologic technologists, who operate imaging equipment, not by a health unit coordinator.
ww.Performing lab tests on blood and tissue: Performing lab tests on blood and tissue is the job of laboratory technologists, which differs from the clerical coordination done on a nursing unit.
ww.Dispensing medication to patients on the: Dispensing medication to patients as ordered is done by nurses and pharmacy staff, while the unit coordinator does not handle or give drugs.

rw: A patient-centered medical home is a care model where a primary care team coordinates all of a patient's care, giving whole-person, continuing and accessible service.

ww.A hospital for home builders and for the: A hospital for home builders and workers hurt on building sites is an occupational injury hospital, which has no connection to the medical home care model.
ww.A building where patients live permanent: A building where patients live permanently with nurses on call describes a residential or nursing facility, not a care model based in primary care.
ww.A program that only handles billing and: A program handling only billing and claims is an insurance administrative function, whereas a medical home is about coordinated clinical care for patients.

rw: A chain of command is the line of authority that shows who reports to whom, so staff know where to take problems and who makes decisions.

ww.A schedule of surgeries and the rooms in: A schedule of surgeries and rooms plans operating room use, which shows timing and place but not who answers to whom in the organization.
ww.A list of patient diagnoses kept for the: A list of diagnoses kept by the records office documents patient conditions, which has no bearing on authority or reporting relationships among staff.
ww.A set of building keys held by the secur: A set of building keys held by security staff is a physical access tool, and it does not describe lines of authority in a healthcare organization.

rw: An organizational chart is a diagram of the structure and reporting lines in an organization, showing positions, departments and who supervises whom.

ww.A graph of hospital revenue showing the: A graph of revenue by service shows financial results, while an organizational chart shows how people and units are arranged and who reports to whom.
ww.A list of medicines kept in the pharmacy: A list of medicines kept in the pharmacy is a formulary or inventory, which describes drugs, not the structure of staff and departments.
ww.A chart of a patient's heart rate, plott: A chart of a patient's heart rate plotted at the bedside is a clinical record of vital signs, not a diagram of an organization.

rw: An ACO is a group of providers that share responsibility for the quality and cost of care for a group of patients, and may share savings when targets are met.

ww.An organization that grows hospital food: Growing hospital food on farms and delivering it to kitchens is a supply operation, which has nothing to do with sharing accountability for patient care quality and cost.
ww.An organization that licenses nurses and: Licensing nurses and approving training courses is done by state boards and regulators, which differ from provider groups that share responsibility for outcomes and spending.
ww.An organization that audits tax returns: Auditing tax returns and checking firms' sums is the job of a tax authority, which has no connection to coordinating patient care among providers.

rw: An HMO is a health plan with a network of providers that usually requires referrals for specialists, with a primary care doctor guiding the member's care.

ww.A government agency that licenses doctor: A government agency that licenses doctors and checks their training is a medical licensing board, not a health plan that organizes a network of providers.
ww.A plan that lets members see any provide: A plan letting members see any provider with no limits and no referral is far more open than an HMO, which restricts care to its network.
ww.A plan that pays only for dental care, s: A plan paying only for dental care is a dental plan, whereas an HMO covers a broad range of medical services through a network.

rw: A PPO is a health plan that lets members see in-network or out-of-network providers, with lower costs in network and higher costs when they go outside.

ww.A plan run by the hospital's cafeteria t: A plan run by the hospital cafeteria for staff meals is a food discount and not health insurance, so it has no link to provider networks.
ww.A plan that covers only emergency visits: A plan covering only emergency visits is limited coverage, whereas a PPO pays for planned care too, including routine visits and specialist services.
ww.A plan that requires members to use one: A plan requiring one clinic only with no cover elsewhere is far more restrictive than a PPO, which allows members to choose providers outside the network.

rw: In-network providers have a contract with the insurer to charge agreed rates, so members usually pay less than they would for out-of-network care.

ww.Providers who refuse insurance and will: Providers who refuse insurance and treat only cash patients are out of the insurer's arrangements, which is the opposite of being in-network with a contract.
ww.Providers who work only at night and are: Working only at night describes a schedule and not a contract, so the hours a provider works do not decide whether they are in-network.
ww.Providers located in a hospital building: The location of a provider's building, even near the insurer's offices, does not decide network status, which depends on a signed contract.

rw: Revenue is money earned from providing services and other sources, such as patient fees, insurer payments, grants and donations, and it flows into the organization.

ww.Money spent on supplies and wages by the: Money spent on supplies and wages is an expense, which flows out of the organization, so it is the opposite of revenue.
ww.Money borrowed from banks to build a new: Money borrowed from banks is a loan, a liability the organization must repay with interest, and it is not earned by providing services.
ww.Money owed to suppliers for goods that h: Money owed to suppliers for delivered goods is accounts payable, a liability, while revenue is what the organization earns from its own services.

rw: An expense is a cost of operating, such as wages, supplies and utilities, which an organization pays out as it delivers care.

ww.Money donated to the hospital by local f: Money donated by local families and firms is a source of income and so counts toward revenue, not a cost of running the hospital.
ww.Money earned from patient care and from: Money earned from patient care and services sold is revenue, so it comes in to the hospital instead of being a cost paid out.
ww.The value of the hospital building, an a: The value of a building the hospital owns is an asset on the balance sheet, which is not itself an expense for operating costs.

rw: A budget is a plan that estimates income and expenses for a period, helping managers set priorities, control spending and compare results with targets.

ww.A list of all hospital employees and the: A list of employees and their job titles is a staff roster, which records people and roles but does not estimate income and expenses.
ww.A report of past insurance claims, sorte: A report of past insurance claims sorted by date records history, while a budget looks ahead and plans for future income and spending.
ww.A record of every patient visit to the h: A record of every patient visit in a year is a log of activity, and a budget instead is a financial plan with expected income and costs.

rw: An operating budget is a plan for day-to-day revenue and expenses for the coming year, covering items such as wages, supplies and utilities.

ww.A plan for buying a new building or majo: A plan for buying a new building or major equipment over many years is a capital budget, not an operating budget for routine yearly activity.
ww.A plan for a patient's treatment, with t: A plan for a patient's treatment with drugs and tests is a care plan, which is clinical and not a financial document for the organization.
ww.A plan for disaster response, such as fl: A plan for disaster response is an emergency preparedness plan, which covers safety procedures instead of estimating regular revenue and expenses for the year.

rw: A capital budget is a plan for major, long-lasting purchases such as buildings or equipment, which are used for many years and cost a lot.

ww.A plan for staff holidays and leave date: A plan for staff holidays and leave dates is a scheduling matter, not a budget for large, long-lasting purchases like buildings or equipment.
ww.A plan for monthly office supplies, smal: A plan for monthly supplies, small repairs and routine purchases belongs in the operating budget, since these are regular, short-term costs, not major capital items.
ww.A plan for a single patient's bill, show: A plan for one patient's bill showing charges per service is an itemized statement, which records charges for an individual instead of planning organizational investment.

rw: A new MRI machine is a major, long-lasting purchase costing a large sum and used for years, so it is a capital budget item.

ww.Buying paper for the printer: Buying paper for the printer is a small, routine supply purchase used up quickly, so it belongs in the operating budget, not the capital budget.
ww.Paying the weekly wages: Weekly wages are a regular recurring cost of day-to-day operations, so they are paid from the operating budget and not the capital budget.
ww.Paying monthly power bills: Monthly power bills are recurring utility expenses of daily operations, so they fall in the operating budget instead of the capital budget.

rw: A fixed cost stays the same regardless of the number of patients, and rent is the usual example because it is due even in a very quiet month.

ww.The cost of lab tests per patient, which: Lab test costs per patient rise with each patient seen, so they change with volume and are variable costs, not fixed ones.
ww.The cost of gloves, masks and other supp: Gloves, masks and supplies used per patient grow with the number of visits, which makes them variable costs instead of fixed costs.
ww.Overtime paid on busy days to staff who: Overtime paid on busy days rises with workload and falls when visits drop, so it varies with activity and is not a fixed cost.

rw: A variable cost changes with the number of patients, as medical supplies do, because more visits use more gloves, dressings and other consumables.

ww.The salary of the office manager who run: An office manager's salary is paid whether the clinic sees ten patients or a hundred, so it is a fixed cost, not a variable one.
ww.The yearly insurance premium on the buil: A yearly insurance premium on the building is the same for any patient count, which is the definition of a fixed cost, not a variable one.
ww.The monthly lease on the building where: A monthly lease is due in the same amount regardless of how many patients attend, so it is a fixed cost and not variable.

rw: Total cost equals fixed cost plus variable cost: $20,000 plus 800 times $15, which is $12,000, giving $32,000 for the month.

ww.$35,000: Using $35,000 implies about 1,000 visits ($20,000 plus $15,000), or an error in the count, but 800 visits at $15 give only $12,000 of variable cost.
ww.$12,000: Using $12,000 counts only the variable cost, 800 times $15, and leaves out the $20,000 in fixed costs that the clinic pays every month.
ww.$20,015: Using $20,015 adds the cost of a single visit ($15) to the fixed costs, but the variable cost must be multiplied by all 800 visits.

rw: Reimbursement is payment that providers receive from insurers or programs for services, which covers some or all of the cost of care they delivered.

ww.A tax paid by hospitals to the state eac: A tax paid by hospitals on their income is a government charge, which flows out of the hospital, whereas reimbursement is payment received for care given.
ww.A fee patients pay to enter a hospital,: A fee patients pay to enter a hospital is an admission charge, whereas reimbursement comes from insurers or programs after services are given.
ww.A discount on equipment purchases for la: A discount on equipment for buying groups is a purchasing saving on costs, and it is not payment received for providing patient services.

rw: Accounts receivable is money owed to a provider for services already delivered, such as bills sent to insurers and patients that have not yet been paid.

ww.Money held in a savings account at a ban: Money held in a savings account is cash on hand, which the provider already has, rather than a debt owed to it by others.
ww.Money set aside for emergencies and held: Money set aside for emergencies in a reserve fund is a savings policy, and it is not owed by customers for services delivered.
ww.Money the provider owes to suppliers for: Money the provider owes to suppliers is accounts payable, which is a liability, the opposite of money owed to the provider.

rw: Accounts payable is money a provider owes to vendors and suppliers for goods and services received but not yet paid for, shown as a liability.

ww.Money the provider earns each year from: Money earned each year from donations is income or revenue, whereas accounts payable is money the provider owes, which is a liability.
ww.Money owed to the provider by insurers f: Money owed to the provider by insurers for care is accounts receivable, an asset, so it is the reverse of accounts payable.
ww.Money patients have paid in advance for: Money patients paid in advance for care is a deposit or deferred revenue, and not an amount the provider owes to vendors.

rw: A charge master is a list of a provider's standard prices for services and items, which serves as the starting point for billing before insurer discounts apply.

ww.A list of employees' pay rates and job g: A list of employees' pay rates and job grades is a pay scale or payroll document, not the list of prices charged for services.
ww.A manager who oversees credit cards for: A manager overseeing credit cards is a finance role, whereas a charge master is a document and not a person.
ww.A machine that charges phones for visito: A machine that charges phones for visitors is a device and has no link to a hospital's price list for services.

rw: Insurers pay less than billed because they negotiate discounted rates with in-network providers, so the allowed amount is lower than the charge on the bill.

ww.Insurers never pay claims, whatever the: Insurers do pay claims for covered care, so the claim that they never pay is false and would not explain a partial payment.
ww.Hospitals always overcharge, so insurers: Saying hospitals always overcharge is an overstatement, and the gap exists mainly because of contracted rates that insurers negotiate with providers in advance.
ww.Patients refuse to pay at all after they: Patients are billed only for their share, and insurers pay at contracted rates before that, so refusal by patients to pay is not why payments are lower.

rw: A variance is the difference between budgeted and actual amounts, which tells managers where spending or revenue differs from the plan and may need action.

ww.A type of insurance plan that covers bus: A type of insurance plan covering business losses is a different financial product and not the budgeting measure comparing planned figures with actual results.
ww.A list of budget rules that staff must f: A list of rules for staff to follow is a policy document, whereas variance is a numerical difference found by comparing budget with actual figures.
ww.A chart of patient ages shown for each h: A chart of patient ages by ward is demographic information, which is unrelated to comparing planned and real financial amounts.

rw: Variance equals actual minus budget: $56,000 minus $50,000 is $6,000, and since spending exceeded the plan, the department is over budget.

ww.$0 over budget: A variance of $0 would mean actual spending matched the budget, but the department spent $56,000 against $50,000, so a difference exists.
ww.$6,000 under budget: A $6,000 difference is right in size but wrong in direction, because spending of $56,000 above the $50,000 budget means over budget, not under.
ww.$106,000 over budget: The figure $106,000 comes from adding $50,000 and $56,000, but variance is the difference between them, which is $6,000, not their sum.

rw: Cost containment means efforts to control and reduce healthcare spending without harming quality, through measures such as efficient purchasing, less waste and better coordination of care.

ww.Ignoring all spending in every departmen: Ignoring spending in every department does nothing to control costs, so it cannot be cost containment, which needs active monitoring and management of spending.
ww.Increasing prices on all services so the: Raising prices on all services increases income but does not control or reduce spending, so it is not cost containment.
ww.Closing every department of the hospital: Closing every department would end the hospital's ability to treat anyone, so it destroys the service instead of controlling costs while keeping quality.

rw: Bulk purchasing lowers the price per unit, and reducing wasted supplies cuts needless spending, so both save money without lowering the quality of care.

ww.Cutting nurse training to save money on: Cutting nurse training saves money now but weakens skills and safety, so quality of care suffers, which fails the aim of containing costs without harm.
ww.Skipping safety checks to save time on t: Skipping safety checks saves time but raises the chance of errors and injuries, which harms care quality and can cost more later.
ww.Delaying all equipment repairs until mac: Delaying all repairs until machines break down risks failures during care and costlier emergency fixes, so it can hurt patients and raise spending.

rw: Capitation is a fixed payment per patient per period regardless of how many services are used, so the provider carries the risk of higher use.

ww.A payment only after a patient recovers,: Paying only after a patient recovers is an outcome-contingent arrangement, not capitation, which pays a set amount up front whatever the patient's result.
ww.A payment made in cash only, handed over: Paying in cash only at the front desk describes a method of payment and not a model that sets a fixed amount per patient.
ww.A payment for each separate service that: A payment for each separate service performed is fee-for-service, which is the opposite of capitation's single fixed amount per patient.

rw: Under fee-for-service, providers are paid separately for each service they perform, such as a visit, test or procedure, so more services means more payment.

ww.Providers are paid only for good outcome: Paying providers only for good outcomes describes value-based or pay-for-performance models, not fee-for-service, which pays for each service regardless of results.
ww.Providers receive one fixed payment per: One fixed payment per patient each year describes capitation, in which payment does not rise with the number of services provided.
ww.Providers work for free and are paid onl: Providers working for free and relying on donations is a charity model, whereas fee-for-service is a standard payment arrangement with insurers and patients.

rw: Value-based care rewards providers for quality and outcomes, so payment depends on how well patients do and not just on how many services are delivered.

ww.A payment approach that charges patients: Charging patients more for each visit is a pricing choice and not value-based care, which links payment to quality and results instead of the volume of visits.
ww.A payment approach that rewards the most: Rewarding the most services whatever the outcome describes fee-for-service incentives, which are the reverse of value-based care that pays for results.
ww.A payment approach that ends insurance f: Ending insurance for all patients of a plan is not a payment approach to reward good care, and it would remove coverage instead.

rw: Break-even analysis finds the number of patients, or volume of services, needed for revenue to equal costs, beyond which the clinic starts to make a profit.

ww.Measuring wait times in the clinic acros: Measuring wait times is an operations and service-quality study, which does not compare revenue with costs to find the point of balance.
ww.Counting equipment that breaks down in t: Counting equipment breakdowns is a maintenance review, and it does not look at revenue, costs or the volume needed to cover them.
ww.Comparing doctors' salaries across the d: Comparing doctors' salaries across departments is a pay comparison, whereas break-even analysis looks at the volume at which revenue covers total costs.

rw: Each visit contributes $90 minus $30, which is $60, so break-even is $18,000 divided by $60, which equals 300 visits.

ww.200 visits: Using 200 visits divides $18,000 by $90 and ignores the $30 supplies cost; each visit contributes only $90 minus $30, which is $60.
ww.600 visits: Using 600 visits divides $18,000 by $30, which is the cost per visit, but the right divisor is the $60 contribution margin per visit.
ww.18,000 visits: Using 18,000 visits would need a contribution of only $1 per visit, but each visit actually contributes $60, so far fewer visits cover the fixed costs.

rw: A deductible is the amount a patient pays for covered care before insurance begins to pay, and it usually resets each plan year.

ww.A monthly payment for insurance, billed: A monthly payment for insurance billed to the policyholder is a premium, which is paid whether or not any care is used, and not a deductible.
ww.A flat fee paid at each visit to a docto: A flat fee paid at each doctor or clinic visit is a copayment, which is charged per service and does not accumulate toward starting coverage.
ww.The maximum an insurer will pay out for: The maximum an insurer will pay in a year is a benefit limit, while a deductible is what the patient pays first.

rw: A copayment is a fixed amount a patient pays for a specific service at the time of care, such as a set fee for each doctor visit.

ww.A monthly insurance payment made to keep: A monthly insurance payment to keep a plan active is a premium, which is paid regardless of whether care is used, not a copay.
ww.A tax on medical services that is paid t: A tax on medical services paid to the state by providers is a government levy, which is not a payment a patient makes at the time of care.
ww.A yearly amount paid before coverage sta: A yearly amount paid before coverage starts is a deductible, which resets each plan year, while a copay is a fixed fee per service.

rw: Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost of care that a patient shares with the insurer after the deductible is met, such as 20 percent.

ww.The monthly cost of insurance paid by th: The monthly cost paid to keep a plan active is a premium, which is separate from coinsurance, which applies only when care is received.
ww.The yearly maximum a patient pays out of: The yearly maximum a patient pays out of pocket is the out-of-pocket maximum, which caps total spending, while coinsurance is the percentage share of each bill.
ww.A flat fee for each visit paid by the pa: A flat fee paid by the patient at each visit is a copayment, which is a fixed dollar amount and not a percentage of the cost.

rw: The patient pays 20 percent of the $1,000 allowed charge, which is 0.20 times $1,000, giving $200, with the insurer paying the rest.

ww.$1,000: Paying $1,000 would mean the patient covers the whole allowed charge, but after the deductible is met the patient pays only the 20 percent coinsurance share.
ww.$20: Paying $20 treats 20 percent as 20 dollars, but coinsurance is a percentage of the allowed charge, so 20 percent of $1,000 is much larger.
ww.$800: An amount of $800 is the share the insurer pays, which is 80 percent of $1,000, while the patient pays the remaining 20 percent, or $200.

rw: Recruitment is finding and attracting qualified people for open jobs, through advertising, job boards, referrals and outreach, before selection and hiring take place.

ww.Ending an employee's contract and handin: Ending an employee's contract and handing over final pay is termination or separation, which is the opposite end of the employment cycle from recruitment.
ww.Reviewing an employee's work and goals o: Reviewing an employee's work and goals once each year is a performance appraisal, which assesses current staff rather than attracting new candidates.
ww.Paying an employee's wages and taxes on: Paying wages and taxes on each payday is payroll, an administrative function for current employees that does not involve finding new staff.

rw: A job description is a document listing the duties and requirements of a position, which helps recruiters, applicants and managers know what the job involves.

ww.A record of a patient's treatment, kept: A record of a patient's treatment kept by the nurse is a medical chart, which documents care of a patient, not the duties of a position.
ww.A list of hospital departments and the m: A list of departments and their managers is an organizational listing, which describes structure rather than the duties and requirements of one particular job.
ww.A schedule of surgeries and the rooms in: A schedule of surgeries and rooms is an operating room plan, and it does not describe the tasks or qualifications of any position.

rw: Credentialing verifies that a clinician's education, license and experience meet standards, so the organization knows the person is qualified to provide care safely.

ww.Printing identification badges for the s: Printing identification badges is an administrative task for security or human resources, which does not verify whether a clinician meets professional standards.
ww.Giving a clinician a new job title and a: Giving a new job title and higher salary after a year is a promotion, which rewards service and does not check qualifications.
ww.Paying a clinician a bonus for work done: Paying a bonus for busy periods is compensation, which rewards effort and does not involve verifying a clinician's education, license or experience.

rw: A license is government permission to practice a profession, granted after meeting set requirements, and practicing without one is generally illegal.

ww.A hospital's tax form filed with the sta: A hospital's yearly tax form filed with the state is a financial filing for the organization, and not a permission for a person to practice.
ww.A discount on supplies given to hospital: A discount on supplies for hospitals that buy in volume is a purchasing arrangement, which has no link to professional permission to practice.
ww.A patient's insurance card shown at the: A patient's insurance card shown at the front desk proves coverage, but it does not grant a professional permission to practice.

rw: A certification is a credential showing that a person passed an exam or met standards in a specialty, which signals added knowledge in that field.

ww.A rule about uniforms that staff must fo: A uniform rule is a dress code policy for staff on duty, which sets appearance standards and does not show that anyone passed an exam.
ww.A form signed by patients to agree to th: A form signed by patients to agree to care is informed consent, which records the patient's agreement and is not a professional credential.
ww.A document that lets a person avoid trai: A certification does not excuse anyone from training, because it proves qualification only after the requirements are met, so letting a person avoid training misstates it.

rw: Orientation teaches policies, safety rules and job expectations, so new hires know how to work safely and what is expected of them from the start.

ww.It hides policies from staff until they: Orientation helps new hires learn policies, so hiding policies from staff for a year would defeat its purpose and put safety and compliance at risk.
ww.It guarantees promotions for all of the: Orientation introduces new hires to the workplace, but it cannot guarantee promotions for everyone, which depend on performance and open positions.
ww.It removes the need for any more trainin: Orientation is only a start, so it does not remove the need for further training as skills and procedures develop on the job.

rw: On-the-job training means learning skills by doing the work with guidance in the workplace, often from a supervisor or experienced colleague who gives feedback.

ww.Learning that avoids practice and uses o: Avoiding practice and using only lectures and reading is classroom study, whereas on-the-job training builds skills through doing real work in the workplace.
ww.Learning by reading at home alone with n: Reading at home alone with no guide or teacher is self-study, which lacks the supervision and hands-on practice that define on-the-job training.
ww.Learning in a classroom away from work,: Learning in a classroom away from work with a lecturing teacher is off-the-job training, which is the opposite of learning in the real work setting.

rw: Continuing education is ongoing learning that helps professionals keep their skills and licenses current, and many licenses require a set number of credit hours.

ww.Education only for new hires in their fi: Education only for new hires in their first weeks is orientation, whereas continuing education is for experienced professionals throughout their careers.
ww.Education that ends at graduation and is: Education that ends at graduation and is never updated is the opposite of continuing education, which exists because medical knowledge changes constantly.
ww.Education about hospital food and the me: Education about hospital food and ward meals is a narrow topic, and continuing education covers many professional subjects, not just meals.

rw: A staffing ratio is the number of patients assigned to each caregiver, such as six patients per nurse, which helps set safe workloads.

ww.The number of beds in the building in us: The number of beds in use each night is a measure of occupancy and capacity, not of how many patients each caregiver looks after.
ww.The ratio of doctors to cars in the park: A ratio of doctors to cars in the parking lot has no relation to patient care or workload, so it is not a staffing ratio.
ww.The percent of staff who retire each yea: The percent of staff who retire each year is an attrition measure, which tracks departures and not how many patients each caregiver handles.

rw: Dividing 24 patients by 4 nurses gives 6 patients per nurse, which is the ratio of patients to nurses on the unit.

ww.20 patients per nurse: Twenty comes from subtracting 4 from 24, but a ratio requires division of patients by nurses, so subtraction does not give patients per nurse.
ww.4 patients per nurse: Four patients per nurse reverses the numbers by using the nurse count as the answer, but 24 patients shared among 4 nurses is more.
ww.96 patients per nurse: Ninety-six comes from multiplying 24 by 4, but sharing patients among nurses needs division, and multiplication gives a figure that is too large.

rw: Overtime is hours worked beyond the standard workweek, often paid at a higher rate such as time and a half, to compensate staff for extra work.

ww.A break for lunch taken during the middl: A lunch break in the middle of a long shift is a rest period, which has no link to hours worked beyond the standard week.
ww.Time off with pay that staff may take on: Time off with pay on holidays and weekends is paid leave, which is the opposite of extra working hours that overtime represents.
ww.The first hour of a shift, when the hand: The first hour of a shift when patients are handed over is a handoff period, and overtime concerns extra hours, not when a shift begins.

rw: A shift schedule is a plan showing which staff work at which times, so that each day and night has the right people on duty.

ww.A plan of insurance premiums due each mo: A plan of insurance premiums due each month is a payment calendar for finance, and it does not show who works at which times.
ww.A plan of patients' meals served on each: A plan of patients' meals on each ward is a menu or dietary schedule, which concerns food and not the working hours of staff.
ww.A plan of a building's layout and its ro: A plan of a building's layout and rooms is a floor plan, which shows space and not the working times of employees.

rw: Patients need care 24 hours a day, every day, so hospitals schedule staff in shifts to make sure nurses and doctors are always present.

ww.Staff prefer to work at night only and n: Staff preferring to work only at night does not explain round-the-clock scheduling, because hospitals need day coverage as well and staff do not all choose nights.
ww.Hospitals close at midnight and open eac: Hospitals do not close at midnight, since emergencies and inpatients need attention overnight, so a closing time would put patients at risk.
ww.Patients only need care on weekdays by d: Patients need care on weekends and holidays too, so saying they only need care on weekdays by day ignores illness and emergencies at all hours.

rw: Employee turnover is the rate at which employees leave and are replaced, and high turnover raises hiring and training costs and can harm continuity of care.

ww.The number of patients treated daily in: The number of patients treated daily in the ER measures patient volume, while turnover concerns employees leaving and being replaced.
ww.The amount of money earned in a year by: The amount of money a worker earns in a year is annual pay, which is a compensation figure and not a rate of departures.
ww.The speed of a hospital's elevators with: The speed of a hospital's elevators is a facility matter that has no relation to how often employees leave a workplace.

rw: Heavy workloads and burnout push nurses to leave, so they are a likely cause of high nurse turnover, along with stress and fatigue.

ww.Strong supportive leadership: Strong supportive leadership makes nurses feel valued and tends to keep them, so it would lower turnover instead of causing it to rise.
ww.Reasonable schedules and help: Reasonable schedules and help ease strain on nurses and encourage them to stay, so they work against turnover and do not explain it.
ww.Chances for professional growth: Chances for professional growth give nurses reasons to stay and build a career, so they reduce turnover and cannot be a cause of nurses leaving.

rw: A performance appraisal is a formal review of an employee's work and goals, giving feedback on results and setting targets for the next period.

ww.A review of a patient's chart by the war: A review of a patient's chart by the ward nurse examines a patient's record, whereas a performance appraisal evaluates an employee's job performance.
ww.A review of a building's safety by inspe: A review of a building's safety by inspectors is a facility inspection, which assesses the premises and not the work of an employee.
ww.A review of the hospital's tax status wi: A review of the hospital's tax status with the state is a regulatory matter for the organization, not an evaluation of an individual employee.

rw: Progressive discipline is a series of increasingly serious steps for repeated misconduct, such as a warning, a written notice, suspension and finally dismissal.

ww.Firing employees without notice for any: Firing employees without notice for any small mistake is the opposite of progressive discipline, which uses graduated steps that give people a chance to improve.
ww.Ignoring all rule breaking by staff on t: Ignoring all rule breaking is not discipline at all, so it cannot be progressive discipline, which responds to misconduct with defined steps.
ww.Rewarding poor behavior with raises and: Rewarding poor behavior with raises and promotions encourages misconduct, whereas progressive discipline responds to repeated misconduct with firmer consequences.

rw: Cultural competence training helps staff respect patients' backgrounds and communicate effectively, which builds trust and improves care for people from many communities.

ww.It lets staff ignore patients' needs whe: Letting staff ignore patients' needs when busy would harm care, and cultural competence training aims for the opposite, which is attentive respect for every patient.
ww.It reduces the need for interpreters, si: Staff cannot learn every language through such training, and interpreters are still needed, so it does not remove their use.
ww.It replaces clinical training for nurses: Cultural competence training adds to clinical training and does not replace the medical education that nurses and doctors need to treat patients safely.

rw: Cross-training teaches employees to perform tasks outside their usual role, so the organization can cover absences and shift workers to where they are needed.

ww.Training that avoids teamwork and keeps: Training that keeps staff apart from each other has no connection to cross-training, which in practice builds flexibility and often supports teamwork.
ww.Training only for managers in the senior: Training limited to senior managers describes leadership development, and cross-training applies to staff at many levels, not just managers.
ww.Training in a different country, with cl: Training in another country in a foreign language is international study, which does not describe learning duties from different roles within the same workplace.

rw: A preceptor is an experienced professional who guides a new or student clinician, giving supervised practice and feedback as the learner builds skills.

ww.A patient who donates blood to the hospi: A patient who donates blood is a blood donor, which is not a professional who guides learners in a clinical setting.
ww.A manager of the billing office who chec: A manager checking insurance claims in the billing office does administrative work, not the teaching and guiding that a preceptor provides.
ww.A hospital volunteer who greets visitors: A volunteer who greets visitors at the door gives a welcome service, but does not teach or supervise new clinicians.

rw: Using safety needles and training in proper disposal reduces accidental sticks and exposure to bloodborne infection, which makes it the policy that protects staff best.

ww.Using needles without containers on the: Using needles without containers leaves sharp items exposed on the wards, which raises the chance of injuries instead of protecting staff.
ww.Skipping safety training for staff who w: Skipping safety training leaves staff unaware of safe handling and disposal, so it raises the risk of needle-stick injuries.
ww.Letting staff recycle needles in open bi: Open bins let sharps be touched or fall out, and needles should go in puncture-resistant containers, so recycling them this way endangers staff.

rw: OSHA sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspecting workplaces and requiring employers to protect workers from hazards.

ww.Sets insurance premiums for the members: Setting insurance premiums for a health plan is done by insurers, and OSHA has no role in pricing coverage.
ww.Licenses all doctors in the country and: Licensing doctors and checking their records is done by state medical boards, while OSHA deals with workplace safety rather than medical licenses.
ww.Pays hospital bills for patients who hav: Paying hospital bills for uninsured patients is a matter of health programs and charity care, not the duty of a workplace safety agency.

rw: Wearing personal protective equipment such as gloves creates a barrier against blood and body fluids, which is a core OSHA-related protection from bloodborne pathogens.

ww.Eating in patient care areas during shif: Eating in patient care areas can carry contamination to food and mouth, so it raises exposure to pathogens instead of protecting workers.
ww.Reusing disposable gloves for all patien: Reusing disposable gloves spreads germs between patients and fails as a barrier, so it breaks safe practice and protects nobody.
ww.Skipping hand washing before and after e: Skipping hand washing before and after each visit lets pathogens spread, so it increases the risk to workers instead of lowering it.

rw: Workers' compensation is insurance that covers medical costs and lost wages for job-related injuries or illness, which protects employees and employers alike.

ww.A bonus for high performance paid to sta: A bonus for high performance is a reward for results, whereas workers' compensation is insurance for job-related injuries and does not depend on performance.
ww.A retirement plan that staff join when t: A retirement plan that staff join at hire is a pension or savings benefit, which provides income later in life, not injury cover.
ww.A fee for new hires that is paid to the: A fee paid by new hires to the hospital is not workers' compensation, which employers fund through insurance for workers hurt on the job.

rw: A mission statement states an organization's purpose and what it does, so staff and the public know why it exists and whom it serves.

ww.A list of employees' duties kept by a wa: A list of employees' duties kept by a ward manager is a role record, which does not state the purpose of the whole organization.
ww.A forecast of next year's profit, set by: A forecast of next year's profit set for the board is a financial projection, which looks at numbers instead of describing why the organization exists.
ww.A record of patients treated in the hosp: A record of patients treated in a year is an activity report, which describes results achieved and not the organization's purpose.

rw: A vision statement describes what an organization hopes to become in the future, giving a direction that guides long-term goals and inspires staff.

ww.A list of rules for staff posted in hosp: A list of rules posted for staff is a set of policies, which tells people how to act and not what the organization aims to become.
ww.A schedule of events for the hospital in: A schedule of events for the coming year is a calendar of activities, which lists dates and not an aspiration for the organization's future.
ww.A summary of last year's results, showin: A summary of last year's results looks back at what happened, while a vision statement looks ahead at what the organization hopes to be.

rw: SWOT analysis reviews strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, looking at internal factors and external factors to guide strategic planning.

ww.A review of supplies, workers, orders, t: The letters in SWOT do not stand for supplies, workers, orders, totals and costs, which is an invented list that has no link to strategy.
ww.A review of salaries, wages, overtime, t: The letters in SWOT do not stand for salaries, wages, overtime, taxes and bonuses, and the analysis is about strategy rather than payroll.
ww.A review of surgeries, wards, operations: Surgeries, wards, operations and treatments is not what SWOT stands for, and the tool is not limited to clinical activities.

rw: A new competitor opening nearby is an external factor that could take patients and revenue, so it is a threat in SWOT terms.

ww.Weakness: A weakness is an internal shortcoming of the hospital, but a competitor opening nearby comes from outside the organization.
ww.Strength: A strength is an internal advantage of the hospital, while a rival opening nearby is an outside event that poses a risk.
ww.Chance: Chance would loosely suggest an opportunity, but a new competitor endangers the hospital's patient base, so it is a threat and not a favorable chance.

rw: A highly trained surgical team is an internal advantage that helps the hospital deliver good care, so it is a strength.

ww.Weakness: A weakness is an internal shortfall, but a highly trained surgical team is a positive resource, so it cannot be a weakness.
ww.Opportunity: An opportunity is a favorable external factor, whereas the surgical team is part of the hospital itself, so it is internal.
ww.Threat: A threat is an external risk, but the surgical team is an internal asset and gives benefit, so it is not a threat.

rw: Strategic planning means setting long-term goals and deciding how to reach them, including the priorities and resources that move the organization toward its vision.

ww.Ordering daily supplies for the wards an: Ordering daily supplies is a routine operational task for the short term, whereas strategic planning concerns long-term direction.
ww.Filing patient charts in the records roo: Filing patient charts is a records task done daily, which lacks the long-term goal setting that strategic planning involves.
ww.Scheduling this week's staff shifts and: Scheduling this week's staff shifts is short-term operational planning, so it differs from strategic planning, which looks years ahead.

rw: A goal is a specific result an organization wants to achieve, which gives staff a clear target and a way to judge progress.

ww.A tool for measuring blood pressure in a: A tool for measuring blood pressure is a medical device, which is unrelated to what an organization sets out to accomplish.
ww.A rule that staff must follow when on du: A rule staff must follow on duty is a policy, which directs behavior and does not name a result to be achieved.
ww.A record of staff hours worked in each p: A record of staff hours worked in each pay period is a timesheet, which documents time and does not state a target outcome.

rw: Reducing wait times to under 20 minutes within six months has a clear number and a deadline, so progress can be measured and checked.

ww.Be the best hospital eventually, as judg: Being the best hospital eventually has no measure and no deadline, and the phrase eventually leaves no way to check whether it has been achieved.
ww.Make patients happier somehow in the mon: Making patients happier somehow gives no number, method or time frame, so nobody could tell whether the goal had been reached.
ww.Improve things when possible, with no de: Improving things when possible has no deadline and no measure of success, so it is too vague to guide action or to evaluate.
